questions.question_text:
The graph of $y = 2\sin x + 3$ and the line $y = 2$ are shown for $0 \le x \le 2\pi$.
[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}[every node/.style={font=\large}]
\begin{axis}[axis lines=middle, xlabel={$x$}, ylabel={$y$},
  xmin=-0.3, xmax=6.9, ymin=-0.6, ymax=6.2,
  xtick={1.5708, 3.1416, 4.7124, 6.2832},
  xticklabels={$\frac{\pi}{2}$, $\pi$, $\frac{3\pi}{2}$, $2\pi$},
  ytick={1, 2, 3, 5},
  samples=200, clip=false,
  axis line style={-{Stealth}}, width=11cm, height=6.5cm]
\addplot[smooth, thick, blue, domain=0:6.2832] {2*sin(deg(x))+3};
\addplot[thick, red, domain=0:6.2832] {2};
\end{axis}
\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]
Solve $2\sin x + 3 = 2$ for $0 \le x \le 2\pi$.

options.why: Dropped the negative sign from $\sin x = -\frac{1}{2}$ and used quadrants 1 and 2.
Used the quadrants where $\cos$ is negative instead of where $\sin$ is negative.
Stopped at the quadrant 3 solution without also taking the quadrant 4 solution.

questions.solution_text:
$2\sin x + 3 = 2$
$\sin x = -\dfrac{1}{2}$
The reference angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, and $\sin x < 0$ in quadrants 3 and 4.
$x = \pi + \dfrac{\pi}{6},\ 2\pi - \dfrac{\pi}{6}$
$x = \dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6}$

questions.question_text:
The graph of $y = 2\sin(2x)+3$ and the line $y = 4$ are shown for $0 \le x \le 2\pi$.
[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}[every node/.style={font=\large}]
\begin{axis}[axis lines=middle, xlabel={$x$}, ylabel={$y$},
  xmin=-0.3, xmax=6.9, ymin=-0.6, ymax=6.2,
  xtick={1.5708, 3.1416, 4.7124, 6.2832},
  xticklabels={$\frac{\pi}{2}$, $\pi$, $\frac{3\pi}{2}$, $2\pi$},
  ytick={1, 3, 4, 5},
  samples=200, clip=false,
  axis line style={-{Stealth}}, width=11cm, height=6.5cm]
\addplot[smooth, thick, blue, domain=0:6.2832] {2*sin(deg(2*x))+3};
\addplot[thick, red, domain=0:6.2832] {4};
\end{axis}
\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]
Solve $2\sin(2x)+3 = 4$ for $0 \le x \le 2\pi$.

options.why: Solved only the first revolution of $u=2x$ instead of the full domain $0 \le u \le 4\pi$.
Found the four values of $u$ but never divided them by $2$ to recover $x$.
Used the quadrants where sine is negative, solving $\sin u = -\frac{1}{2}$ instead.

questions.solution_text:
$2\sin(2x)+3 = 4$
$\sin(2x) = \dfrac{1}{2}$
Let $u = 2x$, so $0 \le u \le 4\pi$.
$u = \dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$
Adding $2\pi$ to each gives two more values inside $0 \le u \le 4\pi$.
$u = \dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{13\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{17\pi}{6}$
$x = \dfrac{\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{13\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{17\pi}{12}$

questions.question_text:
The graph of $y = 2\cos\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$ and the line $y = 1$ are shown for $0 \le x \le 2\pi$.
[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}[every node/.style={font=\large}]
\begin{axis}[axis lines=middle, xlabel={$x$}, ylabel={$y$},
  xmin=-0.3, xmax=6.9, ymin=-2.6, ymax=2.6,
  xtick={1.5708, 3.1416, 4.7124, 6.2832},
  xticklabels={$\frac{\pi}{2}$, $\pi$, $\frac{3\pi}{2}$, $2\pi$},
  ytick={-2, 1, 2},
  samples=200, clip=false,
  axis line style={-{Stealth}}, width=11cm, height=6.5cm]
\addplot[smooth, thick, blue, domain=0:6.2832] {2*cos(deg(x+pi/6))};
\addplot[thick, red, domain=0:6.2832] {1};
\end{axis}
\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]
Solve $2\cos\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)-1 = 0$ for $0 \le x \le 2\pi$.

options.why: Added $\frac{\pi}{6}$ to each value of $u$ instead of subtracting it to undo the translation.
Solved for $u$ and stopped there, never undoing the horizontal translation.
Included $u=\frac{7\pi}{3}$ without checking that it lies outside the domain for $u$.

questions.solution_text:
$2\cos\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)-1 = 0$
$\cos\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}$
Let $u = x+\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, so $\dfrac{\pi}{6} \le u \le \dfrac{13\pi}{6}$.
The reference angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, and $\cos u > 0$ in quadrants 1 and 4.
$u = \dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3}$
The next value, $\dfrac{7\pi}{3}$, is larger than $\dfrac{13\pi}{6}$, so it is rejected.
$x = u - \dfrac{\pi}{6}$
$x = \dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$

options.why: Divided by $-\sqrt{3}$ but kept the ratio positive, solving $\tan x = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$.
Used a reference angle of $\frac{\pi}{3}$ instead of $\frac{\pi}{6}$ for $\tan^{-1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$.
Took only the quadrant 2 solution, forgetting that $\tan$ repeats every $\pi$.

questions.solution_text:
$2-\sqrt{3}\tan x = 3$
$-\sqrt{3}\tan x = 1$
$\tan x = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$
The reference angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, and $\tan x < 0$ in quadrants 2 and 4.
$x = \pi - \dfrac{\pi}{6},\ 2\pi - \dfrac{\pi}{6}$
$x = \dfrac{5\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6}$

questions.question_text:
The graph of $y = 2\cos(2x)+1$ and the line $y = 2$ are shown for $-\pi \le x \le \pi$.
[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}[every node/.style={font=\large}]
\begin{axis}[axis lines=middle, xlabel={$x$}, ylabel={$y$},
  xmin=-3.6, xmax=3.6, ymin=-1.8, ymax=3.8,
  xtick={-3.1416, -1.5708, 1.5708, 3.1416},
  xticklabels={$-\pi$, $-\frac{\pi}{2}$, $\frac{\pi}{2}$, $\pi$},
  ytick={-1, 1, 2, 3},
  samples=200, clip=false,
  axis line style={-{Stealth}}, width=11cm, height=6.5cm]
\addplot[smooth, thick, blue, domain=-3.1416:3.1416] {2*cos(deg(2*x))+1};
\addplot[thick, red, domain=-3.1416:3.1416] {2};
\end{axis}
\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]
Solve $2\cos(2x)+1 = 2$ for $-\pi \le x \le \pi$.

options.why: Used only $-\pi \le u \le \pi$ instead of the full transformed domain $-2\pi \le u \le 2\pi$.
Solved over $0 \le x \le \pi$ only, ignoring the negative half of the given domain.
Found the four values of $u$ but never halved them to recover $x$.

questions.solution_text:
$2\cos(2x)+1 = 2$
$\cos(2x) = \dfrac{1}{2}$
Let $u = 2x$, so $-2\pi \le u \le 2\pi$.
The reference angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, and $\cos u > 0$ in quadrants 1 and 4.
In $0 \le u \le 2\pi$: $u = \dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3}$
Since $\cos u$ is even, the negative half gives $u = -\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ -\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$
$x = \dfrac{u}{2}$
$x = -\dfrac{5\pi}{6},\ -\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$

questions.question_text:
The graph of $y = 4\sin(3x)+6$ and the line $y = 1$ are shown for $0 \le x \le 2\pi$.
[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}[every node/.style={font=\large}]
\begin{axis}[axis lines=middle, xlabel={$x$}, ylabel={$y$},
  xmin=-0.3, xmax=6.9, ymin=-0.6, ymax=11.5,
  xtick={1.5708, 3.1416, 4.7124, 6.2832},
  xticklabels={$\frac{\pi}{2}$, $\pi$, $\frac{3\pi}{2}$, $2\pi$},
  ytick={1, 2, 6, 10},
  samples=200, clip=false,
  axis line style={-{Stealth}}, width=11cm, height=6.5cm]
\addplot[smooth, thick, blue, domain=0:6.2832] {4*sin(deg(3*x))+6};
\addplot[thick, red, domain=0:6.2832] {1};
\end{axis}
\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]
How many solutions does $4\sin(3x)+6 = 1$ have for $0 \le x \le 2\pi$?

options.why: Assumed two solutions in each of the three cycles without checking that $|\sin u| \le 1$.
Read $\sin 3x = -\frac{5}{4}$ as $-\frac{4}{5}$ and then solved only the first cycle.
Assumed the line just touches the curve at its minimum, as happens when the values are equal.

questions.solution_text:
$4\sin(3x)+6 = 1$
$\sin(3x) = -\dfrac{5}{4}$
The sine of any angle lies between $-1$ and $1$, and $-\dfrac{5}{4} < -1$.
The lowest point of the curve is $y=2$, which is still above the line $y=1$.
There are $0$ solutions.

questions.question_text:
The graph of $y = 2\sin\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)$ and the line $y = -\sqrt{3}$ are shown for $0 \le x \le 4\pi$.
[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}[every node/.style={font=\large}]
\begin{axis}[axis lines=middle, xlabel={$x$}, ylabel={$y$},
  xmin=-0.6, xmax=14.6, ymin=-2.6, ymax=2.6,
  xtick={3.1416, 6.2832, 9.4248, 12.5664},
  xticklabels={$\pi$, $2\pi$, $3\pi$, $4\pi$},
  ytick={-2, 2},
  samples=200, clip=false,
  axis line style={-{Stealth}}, width=12cm, height=6.5cm]
\addplot[smooth, thick, blue, domain=0:12.5664] {2*sin(deg(x/2))};
\addplot[thick, red, domain=0:12.5664] {-1.73205};
\node[red, anchor=west] at (axis cs:12.8,-1.73205) {$y=-\sqrt{3}$};
\end{axis}
\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]
Solve $2\sin\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)+\sqrt{3} = 0$ for $0 \le x \le 4\pi$.

options.why: Found the values of $u=\frac{x}{2}$ correctly but never doubled them to recover $x$.
Dropped the negative sign and solved $\sin u = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ before doubling.
Stopped after the quadrant 3 solution instead of also taking the quadrant 4 solution.

questions.solution_text:
$2\sin\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)+\sqrt{3} = 0$
$\sin\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right) = -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$
Let $u = \dfrac{x}{2}$, so $0 \le u \le 2\pi$.
The reference angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, and $\sin u < 0$ in quadrants 3 and 4.
$u = \dfrac{4\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3}$
$x = 2u$
$x = \dfrac{8\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{10\pi}{3}$

questions.question_text:
The graph of $y = 4\cos(2x)$ and the line $y = -2$ are shown for $0 \le x \le \pi$.
[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}[every node/.style={font=\large}]
\begin{axis}[axis lines=middle, xlabel={$x$}, ylabel={$y$},
  xmin=-0.2, xmax=3.5, ymin=-5, ymax=5,
  xtick={0.7854, 1.5708, 2.3562, 3.1416},
  xticklabels={$\frac{\pi}{4}$, $\frac{\pi}{2}$, $\frac{3\pi}{4}$, $\pi$},
  ytick={-4, -2, 4},
  samples=200, clip=false,
  axis line style={-{Stealth}}, width=11cm, height=6.5cm]
\addplot[smooth, thick, blue, domain=0:3.1416] {4*cos(deg(2*x))};
\addplot[thick, red, domain=0:3.1416] {-2};
\end{axis}
\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]
Solve $4\cos(2x)+2 = 0$ for $0 \le x \le \pi$.

options.why: Found the values of $u=2x$ correctly but never halved them to recover $x$.
Dropped the negative sign and solved $\cos u = \frac{1}{2}$ instead.
Used the domain $0 \le u \le \pi$ instead of $0 \le u \le 2\pi$, losing the second solution.

questions.solution_text:
$4\cos(2x)+2 = 0$
$\cos(2x) = -\dfrac{1}{2}$
Let $u = 2x$, so $0 \le u \le 2\pi$.
The reference angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, and $\cos u < 0$ in quadrants 2 and 3.
$u = \dfrac{2\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{4\pi}{3}$
$x = \dfrac{u}{2}$
$x = \dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{2\pi}{3}$
